newsitem.title: GERMANY: Key dates in Helmut Kohl's 14 years in office.
newsitem.headline: Key dates in Helmut Kohl's 14 years in office.

text.p: Helmut Kohl will overtake his political mentor Konrad Adenauer on Thursday to become post-war Germany's longest-serving chancellor.
Here are the most important dates of his chancellorship:

Oct 1, 1982 - Kohl replaces Social Democrat Chancellor Helmut Schmidt after the small Free Democratic Party (FDP) bolts the SPD-led coalition and forms government with Kohl's Christian Democrats (CDU) and Bavarian CSU party.
March 6, 1983 - In an early election, Kohl's CDU/CSU centre-right coalition wins 48.8 percent of the votes and its first popular mandate to govern West Germany.

Nov 22, 1983 - After huge street protests, parliament follows Kohl's urging and approves stationing of U.S. Pershing-II medium-range missiles in West Germany in response to Soviet SS-20 rockets directed towards western Europe.

Sept 22, 1984 - Kohl and French President Francois Mitterrand seal Franco-German reconciliation by holding hands at World War One battlefield of Verdun, symbolising the end of enmity between the two countries.

May 5, 1985 - Kohl and U.S. President Ronald Reagan visit Bitburger Military Cemetary but the ceremony meant as a reconciliation gesture provokes loud protests because Nazi Waffen-SS soldiers are also buried there.

Sept 7, 1987 - Kohl receives East German leader Erich Honecker on his first and only official visit to Bonn. The meeting leads to easing of bilateral relations. Kohl insists Germany's post-war division is still an open question while Honecker argues unification is no longer an issue.

Nov 9, 1989 - After East Germans flood through Hungary and Czechoslovakia to the West, East Germany opens Berlin Wall. Kohl interrupts a trip to Poland to rush to Berlin for a rally with former Chancellor Willy Brandt and Foreign Minister Hans- Dietrich Genscher. Crowd greets him with loud boos.

Nov 28, 1989 - Kohl announces a 10-point programme to bring both German states into a confederation and finally reunite. His allies at home and abroad are surprised by the bold step, which puts him at the head of a groundswell towards unity.
Feb 9, 1990 - Kohl pays lightning visit to Moscow and obtains promise from President Mikhail Gorbachev that Soviet Union will not oppose German reunification.
July 1, 1990 - West Germany's deutschemark becomes legal tender in East Germany in the first step towards unity.
July 16, 1990 - Kohl obtains agreement from Gorbachev that united Germany will remain in NATO and Soviet troops will be withdrawn from eastern Germany by late 1994.
Aug 31, 1990 - The unity treaty on merging East Germany with Bonn's Federal Republic is signed.

Sept 12, 1990 - The "2+4" Treaty granting full sovereignty to the united state is signed in Moscow by both German states and the four wartime allies -- the United States, Soviet Union, Britain and France.

Oct 3, 1990 - The two Germanys merge at midnight with a huge party at Berlin's Reichstag building. East Germany disappears and 144 East Berlin deputies move to Bonn to take up seats in parliament there.
Dec 2, 1990 - Kohl's coalition of CDU/CSU and FDP wins first all-German general election.
June 20, 1991 - Parliament decides by a slim majority to move government to Berlin but leave some ministeries in Bonn. Kohl argues for Berlin.

Feb 7, 1992 - European Union's Maastricht treaty, which Kohl and Mitterrand strongly favour, lays down 1999 as deadline for European monetary union. Treaty agrees to move slowly towards common foreign and defence policy but fails to launch the political union Kohl says is necessary complement to single currency.
Oct 16, 1994 - Coalition wins general election with only 10-seat majority in a parliament of 672 deputies. Kohl forms his fifth government.
May 8, 1995 - Kohl hosts 50-year anniversary gathering of wartime allies in Berlin, where Mitterrand makes emotional speech confirming the friendship of the former enemies.
